items.title: Ray Bryant interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, March 22, 1998
items.q: at night time I played downtown at the Five Spot with guys like Benny Golson

ctx.x: A lot of great musicians including yourself came out of there.

A lot of guys. A lot of guys, yeah. The Heath brothers, you know, Jimmy, Percy, Albert, Tootie; oh Lee Morgan, Bobby Timmons, Benny Golson. Benny and I sort of grew up together you know. And oh, McCoy Tyner, John Coltrane. It’s just full of great musicians.
Is there anything that distinguishes a musician from Philadelphia do you think?

items.title: Benny Golson — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: John – Ray Bryant was 14 years old, the piano player. That guy was a genius... I remember we were out one night at a luncheonette... Ray Bryant got me the gig, because he’s a piano player.

ctx.x: Let’s talk about the kind of repertoire you were performing at this time. What . . . ?

All stock arrangements. One O’Clock Jump by Count Basie, 9:20 Special, Count Basie, Take the “A” Train, Count Basie. Then there was a fellow named Spud Murphy and Van Alexander, that they wrote a lot of stock arrangements. So we were playing a lot of Spud Murphy stuff and Van Alexander stuff. They didn’t print them like the old stocks, which is on small paper, about half the size of that. It was like real professionals used. But they were printed of course. But it looked like you were a professional, and it…

When I met John, I was in high school. I was 16. He was 18. John was playing alto. A kid came to school one day. Said, “Benny, a guy moved into the projects today. Boy, he plays alto just like Johnny Hodges.” That was before Charlie Parker. The barometer was Johnny Hodges and – I forgot the other saxophonist’s name. I said, “What? He plays like John?” He says, “Yeah. He sounds just like him.” I said, “Think you can bring him by the house?” He said, “Yeah.” Next day, the bell rang. Howard came in – Howard played…
